wording: Vitality (Greek, descriptive): Stoic pneuma ('breath') comes in grades — the lowest gives cohesion to inanimate bodies, higher ones account for nature (growth) and soul.
verification_phrases: S07|lowest kind accounts for the cohesion

wording: Vitality (Hebrew Bible, descriptive): Genesis 1:2 rûaḥ is rendered 'a wind from God' in the JPS translation, which notes that others render it 'the spirit of [God]' — the word spans wind, breath and spirit.
locator: Sefaria API, JPS gender-sensitive edition with footnote

wording: Connection/vitality (Christian, descriptive): John 3:8 (WEB) likens being 'born of the Spirit' to the wind that blows where it wants; inspiration: 2 Timothy 3:16 calls Scripture 'God-breathed'.
Vitality (Islamic, descriptive): Qur'an 15:29 describes God breathing into the human of His [created] soul (rūḥ).
Vitality (Chinese, descriptive): qi is described as 'breath-energy' from which organic being and animation emerge; the phenomena the West associates with soul are, in this view, light, refined qi.

Transcendence: mystical experience is defined (SEP) to exclude visions, voices and powers; mysticism covers practices, texts and traditions associated with such experiences, which occur within all world religions.
Connection: African ethics stresses humanity/brotherhood and the common good; animist traditions extend social relations to non-human persons — spirit as connection, reported as belief.

Well-being (demonstrable side): a systematic review reports that religion/spirituality is, on balance, associated with greater well-being and better mental health, with some negative or mixed findings.
counterevidence_limits: Single-author review; mostly observational; publication bias not assessed.

wording: In the Nurses' Health Study (n = 74,534), attending services more than once/week vs never was associated with 33% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.62–0.71).
counterevidence_limits: Women, mostly white US nurses; self-reported attendance.

wording: A meta-analysis of prospective cohorts found religiosity/spirituality associated with reduced mortality in initially healthy populations (combined HR 0.82, 0.76–0.87) but not in diseased populations (HR 0.98, 0.94–1.01).
Many 'spirituality' measures are contaminated with mental-health and positive-character items, making some spirituality–health correlations tautological.
counterevidence_limits: Published replies (listed in PubMed) dispute this; not read.

wording: For HR 0.67, the E-value is 2.35 (rare-outcome) or 1.97 after common-outcome conversion (outcome risk 18%); CI-limit E-values 2.17 / 1.85.
counterevidence_limits: An E-value bounds confounding; it does not detect it.

wording: Corrected confounding simulation: with no causal effect and an unmeasured confounder at strength E on both associations (worst-case allocation), the crude RR was 0.760 vs observed 0.758; at 0.9·E it was 0.812 (cannot explain the association); weak confounding (1.2) gave 0.977.
counterevidence_limits: Binary confounder; no selection or measurement error modelled.

wording: That religious participation causally lowers mortality is a hypothesis: it requires that unmeasured confounding be weaker than RR ≈ 1.97 on both associations, which has not been tested here.
counterevidence_limits: Reverse causation (healthier people attend more) is a live alternative.

wording: Spirit as vitality, transcendence, connection or inspiration is not shown or refuted by the well-being data; those data concern measurable practices and associations, kept separate per the framework.
